<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" ?>
<Page
    x:Class="SDKTemplate.MainPage"
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    xmlns:local="using:SDKTemplate"
    xmlns:d="http://schemas.microsoft.com/expression/blend/2008"
    xmlns:mc="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/markup-compatibility/2006"
    mc:Ignorable="d">

    <Page.Resources>
        <Style x:Key="ScenarioListBoxItemStyle" TargetType="ListBoxItem">
            <Setter Property="Padding" Value="4,8"/>
        </Style>
    </Page.Resources>

    <Grid Background="{ThemeResource ApplicationPageBackgroundThemeBrush}">
        <SplitView x:Name="Splitter" IsPaneOpen="True" DisplayMode="Inline">
            <SplitView.Pane>
                <RelativePanel Margin="10,0,0,0">
                    <TextBlock x:Name="SampleTitle" Text="Sample Title Here"
                               Style="{StaticResource SubtitleTextBlockStyle}"
                               TextWrapping="Wrap" Margin="0,10,0,0"/>
                    <ListBox x:Name="ScenarioControl" SelectionChanged="ScenarioControl_SelectionChanged"
                             AutomationProperties.Name="Scenarios"
                             SelectionMode="Single" HorizontalAlignment="Left"
                             Background="Transparent" BorderThickness="0"
                             VerticalAlignment="Top"
                             RelativePanel.Below="SampleTitle" Margin="0,10,0,0"
                             RelativePanel.Above="FooterPanel">
                        <ListBox.ItemTemplate>
                            <DataTemplate x:DataType="local:Scenario">
                                <TextBlock Text="{x:Bind Title}" TextWrapping="Wrap"/>
                            </DataTemplate>
                        </ListBox.ItemTemplate>
                    </ListBox>
                    <StackPanel x:Name="FooterPanel" Orientation="Vertical"
                                RelativePanel.AlignBottomWithPanel="True">
                        <TextBlock Text="© Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved."
                                   Style="{StaticResource CaptionTextBlockStyle}"
                                   Margin="0,10,0,0" TextWrapping="Wrap"/>
                        <StackPanel Orientation="Horizontal" Margin="0,4,0,10">
                            <HyperlinkButton Content="Trademarks" Tag="http://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?LinkID=623755"
                                             Click="Footer_Click" FontSize="12"/>
                            <TextBlock Text="|" VerticalAlignment="Center" Margin="4,0"/>
                            <HyperlinkButton Content="Privacy" Tag="http://privacy.microsoft.com"
                                             Click="Footer_Click" FontSize="12"/>
                        </StackPanel>
                    </StackPanel>
                </RelativePanel>
            </SplitView.Pane>
            <RelativePanel>
                <Frame x:Name="ScenarioFrame" Margin="5"
                       RelativePanel.AlignTopWithPanel="True"
                       RelativePanel.Above="StatusPanel"
                       RelativePanel.AlignRightWithPanel="True"
                       RelativePanel.AlignLeftWithPanel="True"/>
                <StackPanel x:Name="StatusPanel" Orientation="Vertical"
                            RelativePanel.AlignBottomWithPanel="True"
                            RelativePanel.AlignRightWithPanel="True"
                            RelativePanel.AlignLeftWithPanel="True">
                    <TextBlock x:Name="StatusLabel" Margin="10,0,0,10"
                               TextWrapping="Wrap" Text="Status:"/>
                    <Border x:Name="StatusBorder" Margin="0,0,0,0" Visibility="Collapsed">
                        <ScrollViewer VerticalScrollMode="Auto" VerticalScrollBarVisibility="Auto" MaxHeight="200">
                            <TextBlock x:Name="StatusBlock" FontWeight="Bold"
                                       AutomationProperties.LiveSetting="Assertive"
                                       Margin="10,10,10,20" TextWrapping="Wrap"/>
                        </ScrollViewer>
                    </Border>
                </StackPanel>
            </RelativePanel>
        </SplitView>
        <StackPanel Orientation="Horizontal" VerticalAlignment="Top" HorizontalAlignment="Left">
            <ToggleButton x:Name="HamburgerButton" Click="Button_Click" VerticalAlignment="Top">
                <FontIcon FontFamily="Segoe MDL2 Assets" Glyph=""/>
            </ToggleButton>
            <TextBlock Text="Windows App SDK Sample" Style="{StaticResource CaptionTextBlockStyle}"
                       VerticalAlignment="Center" Margin="8,0,0,0"/>
        </StackPanel>
    </Grid>
</Page>

data.reasoningText:
The output.json shows that only 11 files were generated. This corresponds to: App, MainPage, MainWindow, ContentSelector, LogView, and their .g.i.cs equivalents plus the GlobalUsings.g.cs. But the Scenario*.xaml files weren't generated.

The XAML compiler only ran on some files - it seems like it stopped after processing LogView.xaml and didn't get to the Scenario*.xaml files. Looking at the error message again - "Could not find a part of the path" for `Scenario1_SimplestAdaptiveStreaming.g.i.cs`.

Wait, I think I understand now. 

The XAML compiler creates subdirectories matching the namespace structure when writing generated files - App.g.i.cs goes directly to `win-x64\`, ContentSelector.g.i.cs goes to `win-x64\Controls\`, and LogView.g.i.cs goes to `win-x64\Logging\`. Since Scenario1_SimplestAdaptiveStreaming.xaml is at the project root, its generated file should go directly to `win-x64\`, but the compiler is failing because that directory path doesn't exist or can't be written to.

Looking at the generated files, I'm counting 11 total - App, MainPage, MainWindow, ContentSelector, and LogView each have both .g.cs and .g.i.cs variants, plus GlobalUsings.g.cs. But Scenario1_SimplestAdaptiveStreaming.g.i.cs is missing from this list, which suggests the compiler never successfully generated it due to the path error.

The real issue is likely that the Scenario*.xaml files were ported from UWP and reference styles like `SampleHeaderTextStyle` and `ScenarioDescriptionTextStyle` as `StaticResource` - but these styles don't exist in the WinUI 3 project since they were originally defined in a merged resource dictionary in the UWP App.xaml.

Looking more closely at the error message itself - "Could not find a part of the path" suggests an intermediate directory in the generated file path doesn't exist, or there's an invalid character in the filename. The error is being thrown during MarkupCompilePass1 when trying to write the generated code-behind file, which means the compilation might have failed earlier but the real error is being masked by this file path issue. that shouldn't be the issue. Let me examine the actual Scenario XAML files to see if there are any compatibility problems with WinUI 3.

Good progress! The build is getting much further now - the path issue is resolved by building from Z:. Now I see real compiler errors:

1. **HttpClient, HttpRequestMessage, HttpResponseMessage ambiguous** - need to disambiguate between `System.Net.Http` and `Windows.Web.Http`. Since the code uses Windows HTTP types, I need to add `using` aliases or fully qualify the types.

2. **IHttpFilter interface not implemented** - in `AdaptiveMediaSourceHttpFilterLogger.cs` and `Scenario3_RequestModification.xaml.cs`, there are classes implementing `IHttpFilter` but the `SendRequestAsync` method has a different signature.


3. The `WMC9999 Object reference not set` error at the end is likely a cascading issue from the compilation failures above. The root cause is that implicit usings in .NET 10 automatically include `System.Net.Http`, which conflicts with the `Windows.Web.Http` namespace the code relies on. I can resolve this by adding a `using` alias to explicitly map `HttpClient` to the Windows version at the top of affected files.

Now I need to check what's happening with the `IHttpFilter.SendRequestAsync` method signature to see if there's a mismatch between the interface definition and the implementation.

data.reasoningText:
The problem is clear now. The `ImplicitUsings` in .NET includes `using System.Net.Http;` which conflicts with `Windows.Web.Http`. These two namespaces have types with the same names:
- `System.Net.Http.HttpClient` vs `Windows.Web.Http.HttpClient`
- `System.Net.Http.HttpRequestMessage` vs `Windows.Web.Http.HttpRequestMessage`
- `System.Net.Http.HttpResponseMessage` vs `Windows.Web.Http.HttpResponseMessage`

The `IHttpFilter.SendRequestAsync(HttpRequestMessage request)` method - this is `Windows.Web.Http.HttpRequestMessage`, and `Windows.Web.Http.HttpResponseMessage` - but the ambiguous reference error means the compiler doesn't know which `HttpRequestMessage` / `HttpResponseMessage` to use.


I can fix this by either adding using aliases for the Windows.Web.Http types or removing System.Net.Http from the implicit usings. The cleanest solution is to exclude System.Net.Http from the csproj's implicit usings since this project relies on Windows.Web.Http instead, or add a file-level alias to disambiguate the types.

Let me look at how the WinUI 3 build system calculates the IntermediateOutputPath. Looking at the interop targets, I need to understand what's happening.

When the build runs with `-p:Platform=x64`, MSBuild evaluates:
- `BaseIntermediateOutputPath` = `obj\` (default)
- `IntermediateOutputPath` = `obj\x64\Debug\net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0\win-x64\` (set by packaging targets)

When I override `IntermediateOutputPath` to `obj\$(Configuration)\$(TargetFramework)\$(RuntimeIdentifier)\`:


- On first evaluation: `obj\Debug\net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0\win-x64\`
- But then the XAML compiler targets also append to this, creating: `obj\Debug\net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0\win-x64\net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0\win-x64\`

The problem is that the WinUI packaging targets set `IntermediateOutputPath` after my property, so they override it, but when they see it's already set, they use it as a base and the XAML compiler then appends the same path components again.

Looking at the actual error message, the path is doubled: `win-x64\net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0\win-x64\`. This tells me my `IntermediateOutputPath` override is being used, but then the XAML compiler is treating it as a base and adding `Configuration + TFM + RID` on top of it, creating the nested duplication. When I set `IntermediateOutputPath` explicitly, the XAML compiler seems to be appending its own path construction logic instead of respecting the override.

Let me compare the actual error paths to understand what's happening: without the override, the path is `obj\Debug\net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0\win-x64\` at 262 characters, but with `Platform=x64` and no override, it becomes `obj\x64\Debug\net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0\win-x64\` at 266 characters. The core issue is that the path construction is fundamentally broken when I try to override it.

I'm exploring whether I can override `BaseIntermediateOutputPath` to something minimal like `_` and let the build system append the Platform, Configuration, TFM, and RID components naturally. If I use `_` instead of `obj`, the path would be `_\x64\Debug\net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0\win-x64\` which is only 49 characters, but even combined with the other components that still totals 265 characters—still over the limit. I'm now considering whether a path junction or symlink could help bypass the character limit entirely.

Actually, what if I point `BaseIntermediateOutputPath` to an external location with a much shorter path? Using something like `C:\tmp\as\` would give me only 10 characters, and the full path would be around 57 characters, bringing the total to about 109 characters—well under the 260-character threshold. I'm testing this approach by setting the property to an external path, though I need to remember the constraint about not using temp directories and instead use something like `B:\i\` as the base.

Still failing with a path issue, but now for the XAML source file path, not the generated file. The error says "Could not find a part of the path" for `B:\...\obj\Debug\net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0\win-x64\Scenario1_SimplestAdaptiveStreaming.xaml`. 

The `BaseIntermediateOutputPath` is being used for the generated files, but the XAML compiler is also looking for the source XAML file in the intermediate directory. Wait, it's looking for `Scenario1_SimplestAdaptiveStreaming.xaml` in the obj directory. 

That's the copy of the XAML file that gets placed there during the build. The problem is that this copy is still being written to the old `obj` directory instead of the redirected `B:\i\` location, so `BaseIntermediateOutputPath` didn't fully redirect the XAML compiler's output.

Looking at the actual path length: the base directory plus `obj\Debug\net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0\win-x64\` plus the filename comes to exactly 260 characters, which exceeds the 259-character limit that the XAML compiler enforces. So the XAML file copy itself—not just the generated code-behind files—needs to be at a shorter path.

If I set `BaseIntermediateOutputPath=B:\i\`, the new `IntermediateOutputPath` would become `B:\i\x64\Debug\net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0\win-x64\`, which should be significantly shorter.

But the error message still shows `obj\Debug`, not the `B:\i\` path, which means the `BaseIntermediateOutputPath` override isn't taking effect. The XAML compiler is still writing to the default `obj\` location. I'm wondering if the `-t:Rebuild` flag in the validator is causing the `BaseIntermediateOutputPath` to be evaluated differently or ignored entirely.

Looking at the actual error paths, I notice the Platform override worked—the `x64\` subdirectory disappeared—but the `BaseIntermediateOutputPath` change from `B:\i\` back to `obj\` suggests it's only working for some targets, not the XAML compilation step.

The XAML file path is hitting exactly 260 characters, which is right at the Windows MAX_PATH boundary. The .NET Framework XAML compiler might be stricter about this limit than other tools, treating 260 as the hard cutoff rather than allowing it as a valid length. I'm calculating the full path length by adding the base directory (174 characters including the trailing backslash) to the file path components (85 characters), which gives me 259 characters total—just under the 260-character limit, so this should work.

But I need to consider that the .NET Framework XAML compiler might have stricter path length restrictions than the native MAX_PATH, so let me try setting `BaseIntermediateOutputPath=B:\i\` and running a clean build to see if that helps.

---
name: winui3-parity-check
description: "Verify that a migrated **WinUI 3** app faithfully replicates the **original UWP** app, scenario by scenario, with screenshots and a structural control-coverage gate. Run as the final step of a UWP→WinUI 3 migration (after the build is clean and the app launches). Produces a behavioral baseline from the UWP source, drives the running WinUI 3 app, and reports per-feature PASS/PARTIAL/FAIL so gaps can be fixed before declaring done."
---

## What this skill does

A clean build and a process that stays alive prove almost nothing about *fidelity*.
A page can compile, launch, and survive 10 seconds while every button is dead or an
entire scenario is missing. This skill closes that gap: it turns the **original UWP
app** into a per-scenario **feature checklist + screenshots**, then drives the
**migrated WinUI 3 app** through the same scenarios and grades each one.

It is the verification counterpart to `winui-uwp-migration` (which does the
transformation). Run it **last**, after `Validate-UwpMigration.ps1` reports PASS.

Three scripts do the mechanical work; your judgement fills the gaps the structural
gate can't see (visual layout, exact behaviour).

| Script | Role |
|---|---|
| `scripts/Extract-UwpFeatureChecklist.ps1` | Parse the UWP **source** → `checklist.json` + `info.md`. The ground-truth feature list. No UWP build needed. |
| `scripts/Capture-AppScenarios.ps1` | Drive a **running** app scenario-by-scenario (title-driven nav) → per-scenario screenshot + UIA tree. Works on the UWP app *and* the WinUI 3 app. |
| `scripts/Compare-Parity.ps1` | Grade the WinUI 3 capture against the checklist → `PARITY-REPORT.md` + PASS/FAIL exit code. |

## Prerequisites

- The WinUI 3 migration is built and launches (`winui-uwp-migration` Step 4 PASS).
- `winapp` CLI on PATH (drives + screenshots any packaged app via UI Automation).
- The original UWP **source** is available (the migration skill preserves it; the
  benchmark scenarios point at `...\Samples\<Name>\cs\` + sibling `shared\`).

## Process

### Step 1 — Extract the feature checklist (always)

Derive the ground-truth list of scenarios + controls from the **UWP source**. This
never builds or runs anything, so it always works.

```powershell
& "<skill-root>/scripts/Extract-UwpFeatureChecklist.ps1" `
    -Source "<uwp-cs-source-folder>" `
    -OutDir "<winui3-project-root>/parity/baseline"
```

It writes `parity/baseline/checklist.json` (machine-readable) and
`parity/baseline/info.md` (the same `## Scenario N - <title>` + UI-elements format
the benchmark judge consumes). Read the printed summary — it lists every scenario
and its control count. **That count is your target.**

### Step 2 — Capture the UWP golden screenshots (best-effort, cached)

Screenshots of the *original* UWP app are valuable: they reveal things that reading
the source misses — hidden/disabled controls, default selections, dialog layout, real
text. So capture them when you can. But **running a legacy UWP app is the flaky part**
of this whole process, so this step is best-effort and must degrade gracefully.

**First, reuse any cached goldens.** If `parity/baseline/screenshots/` already exists
(from a prior run or committed into the baseline), do **not** rebuild the UWP app — use
the cached images. The original app is static; capture once, reuse forever.

**Otherwise, try to launch it via the `uwp-app-runner` skill.** It builds, installs
dependencies, registers, and launches the UWP app, returning a structured result:

```powershell
$r = & "<uwp-app-runner-skill>/scripts/Invoke-UwpApp.ps1" `
        -Source "<original-uwp-cs-source-folder>" -Json | ConvertFrom-Json

if ($r.ok) {
    & "<skill-root>/scripts/Capture-AppScenarios.ps1" `
        -App $r.pid `
        -OutDir "<winui3-project-root>/parity/baseline" `
        -Checklist "<winui3-project-root>/parity/baseline/checklist.json"
    # parity/baseline/screenshots/ now holds the golden images — cache them.
} else {
    # Expected for many legacy samples (e.g. crash 0xc000027b / 0xe0434352 at startup).
    Write-Host "UWP golden capture skipped ($($r.stage)): $($r.detail)"
    # Proceed with the source-derived checklist from Step 1 as the baseline.
}
```

> **Do not block on this step.** A live UWP app gives a richer visual reference, but the
> Step 1 checklist (derived from source, always available) is the dependable baseline.
> If the runner reports a `launch` crash, that is a property of the legacy app on this
> OS — not a migration defect — so continue to Step 3.

### Step 3 — Run the WinUI 3 app and capture its scenarios

Launch the migrated app with `winapp run` and capture the **PID** from its output.
Then drive it through the same scenarios:

```powershell
winapp run "<winui3-build-output-folder>"      # note the PID it prints
& "<skill-root>/scripts/Capture-AppScenarios.ps1" `
    -App <winui3-pid> `
    -OutDir "<winui3-project-root>/parity/winui3" `
    -Checklist "<winui3-project-root>/parity/baseline/checklist.json"
```

Navigation is **title-driven** (`winapp ui invoke "<scenario title>"`), so it works
whether your shell is a `NavigationView`, `ListView`, `TabView`, or the UWP-style
`ListBox`. For this to be reliable, the migrated app's nav items must carry the
**same titles** as the source scenarios — keep them verbatim (the migration skill's
navigation invariants already require this).

### Step 4 — Grade parity and fix gaps (mandatory gate)

🛑 **You are not done until `Compare-Parity.ps1` exits 0 (PASS).**

```powershell
& "<skill-root>/scripts/Compare-Parity.ps1" `
    -Checklist "<winui3-project-root>/parity/baseline/checklist.json" `
    -Candidate "<winui3-project-root>/parity/winui3"
```

It writes `parity/winui3/PARITY-REPORT.md` and grades each scenario:

- **pass** — reachable (non-blank screenshot) and ≥80% of the baseline controls
  appear in the captured UIA tree.
- **partial** — reachable and ≥40% coverage. Recognizable but missing controls.
- **fail** — blank/unreachable, or <40% coverage. A dropped or broken scenario.

**For every `partial` / `fail` row:**

1. Open `PARITY-REPORT.md` → read the "Controls not found" list for that scenario.
2. Navigate the running app to that scenario and inspect:
   ```powershell
   winapp ui invoke "<scenario title>" -a <pid>; winapp ui inspect -a <pid> --interactive
   ```
3. Compare `parity/winui3/screenshots/NN_<slug>.png` against the baseline screenshot
   (and the UWP source page) using your own vision — confirm the **visual layout**
   and that each control **does what the UWP handler did**, not just that it exists.
4. Add the missing control / wire up the dead handler in the WinUI 3 page. If a
   control is genuinely unsupported on WinUI 3 desktop, it must already be recorded
   in `MIGRATION-DEFERRED.md` — a deferred scenario is expected to drop, not a defect.
5. Rebuild, re-run Step 3 (re-capture), re-run Step 4. Repeat until PASS.

After PASS, the parity is verified. `parity/baseline/info.md` + screenshots also
double as a reusable behavioral baseline for future regression checks.

## Why structural coverage is necessary but not sufficient

The gate matches a control as "present" when its `AutomationProperties.AutomationId`,
name, or label text appears in the captured UIA tree. That catches the dominant
migration failure — **silently dropped scenarios and controls** — deterministically.
It cannot, by itself, prove a button's *click handler* produces the right result or
that the layout looks right. Those you confirm with the screenshots and the source.
**Set `AutomationProperties.AutomationId` on every interactive control** so the match
is reliable (it also helps the benchmark's own UI checks).

## Critical rules

- **Run after the migration build is clean.** Parity on a broken build is noise.
- **Do not rephrase scenario titles.** Title-driven nav and the checklist both key on
  the verbatim source titles. Trivial capitalization/punctuation cleanup only.
- **Do not delete or renumber checklist scenarios** to make the gate pass. A missing
  scenario is a `fail` to fix, not a row to remove. Deferred scenarios belong in
  `MIGRATION-DEFERRED.md`, not deleted from the checklist.
- **Blank screenshot = fail.** A scenario that renders an empty page is
  indistinguishable from a crash. Device-dependent pages must show a visible fallback
  (see `winui-uwp-migration` "Defensive UI") so they capture a non-blank frame.
- **Don't fake coverage with placeholder controls.** A control must be the real,
  wired-up equivalent of the source control, not an empty look-alike.

---

## What this skill does

A clean build and a process that stays alive prove almost nothing about *fidelity*.
A page can compile, launch, and survive 10 seconds while every button is dead or an
entire scenario is missing. This skill closes that gap: it turns the **original UWP
app** into a per-scenario **feature checklist + screenshots**, then drives the
**migrated WinUI 3 app** through the same scenarios and grades each one.

It is the verification counterpart to `winui-uwp-migration` (which does the
transformation). Run it **last**, after `Validate-UwpMigration.ps1` reports PASS.

Three scripts do the mechanical work; your judgement fills the gaps the structural
gate can't see (visual layout, exact behaviour).

| Script | Role |
|---|---|
| `scripts/Extract-UwpFeatureChecklist.ps1` | Parse the UWP **source** → `checklist.json` + `info.md`. The ground-truth feature list. No UWP build needed. |
| `scripts/Capture-AppScenarios.ps1` | Drive a **running** app scenario-by-scenario (title-driven nav) → per-scenario screenshot + UIA tree. Works on the UWP app *and* the WinUI 3 app. |
| `scripts/Compare-Parity.ps1` | Grade the WinUI 3 capture against the checklist → `PARITY-REPORT.md` + PASS/FAIL exit code. |

## Prerequisites

- The WinUI 3 migration is built and launches (`winui-uwp-migration` Step 4 PASS).
- `winapp` CLI on PATH (drives + screenshots any packaged app via UI Automation).
- The original UWP **source** is available (the migration skill preserves it; the
  benchmark scenarios point at `...\Samples\<Name>\cs\` + sibling `shared\`).

## Process

### Step 1 — Extract the feature checklist (always)

Derive the ground-truth list of scenarios + controls from the **UWP source**. This
never builds or runs anything, so it always works.

```powershell
& "<skill-root>/scripts/Extract-UwpFeatureChecklist.ps1" `
    -Source "<uwp-cs-source-folder>" `
    -OutDir "<winui3-project-root>/parity/baseline"
```

It writes `parity/baseline/checklist.json` (machine-readable) and
`parity/baseline/info.md` (the same `## Scenario N - <title>` + UI-elements format
the benchmark judge consumes). Read the printed summary — it lists every scenario
and its control count. **That count is your target.**

the source misses — hidden/disabled controls, default selections, dialog layout, real
text. So capture them when you can. But **running a legacy UWP app is the flaky part**
of this whole process, so this step is best-effort and must degrade gracefully.

```powershell
        -App $r.pid `
        -OutDir "<winui3-project-root>/parity/baseline" `

    # parity/baseline/screenshots/ now holds the golden images — cache them.

    # Expected for many legacy samples (e.g. crash 0xc000027b / 0xe0434352 at startup).
```

> Step 1 checklist (derived from source, always available) is the dependable baseline.

> OS — not a migration defect — so continue to Step 3.

Then drive it through the same scenarios:

```powershell
    -App <winui3-pid> `
    -OutDir "<winui3-project-root>/parity/winui3" `
    -Checklist "<winui3-project-root>/parity/baseline/checklist.json"
```

`ListBox`. For this to be reliable, the migrated app's nav items must carry the

```powershell
    -Candidate "<winui3-project-root>/parity/winui3"
```

  appear in the captured UIA tree.
- **partial** — reachable and ≥40% coverage. Recognizable but missing controls.
- **fail** — blank/unreachable, or <40% coverage. A dropped or broken scenario.

**For every `partial` / `fail` row:**

1. Open `PARITY-REPORT.md` → read the "Controls not found" list for that scenario.
2. Navigate the running app to that scenario and inspect:
   ```powershell
   winapp ui invoke "<scenario title>" -a <pid>; winapp ui inspect -a <pid> --interactive
   ```
3. Compare `parity/winui3/screenshots/NN_<slug>.png` against the baseline screenshot
   (and the UWP source page) using your own vision — confirm the **visual layout**
   and that each control **does what the UWP handler did**, not just that it exists.
4. Add the missing control / wire up the dead handler in the WinUI 3 page. If a
   control is genuinely unsupported on WinUI 3 desktop, it must already be recorded
   in `MIGRATION-DEFERRED.md` — a deferred scenario is expected to drop, not a defect.
5. Rebuild, re-run Step 3 (re-capture), re-run Step 4. Repeat until PASS.

After PASS, the parity is verified. `parity/baseline/info.md` + screenshots also
double as a reusable behavioral baseline for future regression checks.

## Why structural coverage is necessary but not sufficient

The gate matches a control as "present" when its `AutomationProperties.AutomationId`,
name, or label text appears in the captured UIA tree. That catches the dominant
migration failure — **silently dropped scenarios and controls** — deterministically.
It cannot, by itself, prove a button's *click handler* produces the right result or
that the layout looks right. Those you confirm with the screenshots and the source.
**Set `AutomationProperties.AutomationId` on every interactive control** so the match
is reliable (it also helps the benchmark's own UI checks).

## Critical rules

- **Run after the migration build is clean.** Parity on a broken build is noise.
- **Do not rephrase scenario titles.** Title-driven nav and the checklist both key on
  the verbatim source titles. Trivial capitalization/punctuation cleanup only.
- **Do not delete or renumber checklist scenarios** to make the gate pass. A missing
  scenario is a `fail` to fix, not a row to remove. Deferred scenarios belong in
  `MIGRATION-DEFERRED.md`, not deleted from the checklist.
- **Blank screenshot = fail.** A scenario that renders an empty page is
  indistinguishable from a crash. Device-dependent pages must show a visible fallback
  (see `winui-uwp-migration` "Defensive UI") so they capture a non-blank frame.
- **Don't fake coverage with placeholder controls.** A control must be the real,
  wired-up equivalent of the source control, not an empty look-alike.

Looking at the MSBuild output structure for packaged apps, `OutputPath` determines where the final binaries go and defaults to `bin\$(Platform)\$(Configuration)\$(TargetFramework)\$(RuntimeIdentifier)\`, which is where the AppX layout gets nested. Setting `OutDir` might give me more direct control over this.

The current debug manifest path is around 260 characters, which is too long. I'm trying to shorten `OutputPath` to something like `B:\o\x64\Debug\` to reduce the overall path length.

When I previously used `OutputPath=B:\o\$(Configuration)\$(Platform)\`, the `dotnet run` command failed because it defaulted to `AnyCPU` platform, resulting in `B:\o\Debug\AnyCPU\...`. But if I explicitly set `Platform=x64`, the output would be at `B:\o\Debug\x64\...`, which is much shorter. Let me test this approach with the explicit platform parameter.

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>WinExe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0</TargetFramework>
    <TargetPlatformMinVersion>10.0.17763.0</TargetPlatformMinVersion>
    <RootNamespace>AdaptiveStreaming</RootNamespace>
    <ApplicationManifest>app.manifest</ApplicationManifest>
    <Platforms>x86;x64;ARM64</Platforms>
    <RuntimeIdentifier Condition="'$(RuntimeIdentifier)' == ''">win-$([System.Runtime.InteropServices.RuntimeInformation]::ProcessArchitecture.ToString().ToLowerInvariant())</RuntimeIdentifier>
    <PublishProfile Condition="Exists('Properties\PublishProfiles\win-$(Platform).pubxml')">win-$(Platform).pubxml</PublishProfile>
    <UseWinUI>true</UseWinUI>
    <WinUISDKReferences>false</WinUISDKReferences>
    <EnableMsixTooling>true</EnableMsixTooling>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <!-- Shorten paths to stay within MAX_PATH for package registration -->
    <BaseIntermediateOutputPath>B:\i\</BaseIntermediateOutputPath>
    <OutputPath>B:\o\$(Configuration)\$(Platform)\</OutputPath>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <Using Remove="System.Net.Http" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <Content Include="Assets\SplashScreen.scale-200.png" />
    <Content Include="Assets\LockScreenLogo.scale-200.png" />
    <Content Include="Assets\Square150x150Logo.scale-200.png" />
    <Content Include="Assets\Square44x44Logo.scale-200.png" />
    <Content Include="Assets\Square44x44Logo.targetsize-24_altform-unplated.png" />
    <Content Include="Assets\Square44x44Logo.targetsize-48_altform-lightunplated.png" />
    <Content Include="Assets\StoreLogo.png" />
    <Content Include="Assets\AppIcon.ico" />
    <Content Include="Assets\Wide310x150Logo.scale-200.png" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <Manifest Include="$(ApplicationManifest)" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <!--
    Defining the "Msix" ProjectCapability here allows the Single-project MSIX Packaging
    Tools extension to be activated for this project even if the Windows App SDK Nuget
    package has not yet been restored.
  -->
  <ItemGroup Condition="'$(DisableMsixProjectCapabilityAddedByProject)'!='true' and '$(EnableMsixTooling)'=='true'">
    <ProjectCapability Include="Msix" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <!--
    Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp adds first-class support for
    `dotnet run` on packaged WinUI apps: it hooks the .NET CLI Run target to
    register a debug identity via the winapp CLI and launch the app with
    package identity (AUMID).
    Set <EnableWinAppRunSupport>false</EnableWinAppRunSupport> in a
    <PropertyGroup> above to opt out.
  -->
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools" Version="10.0.28000.1839" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK" Version="2.2.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp" Version="0.3.2" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <!--
    Defining the "HasPackageAndPublishMenuAddedByProject" property here allows the Solution
    Explorer "Package and Publish" context menu entry to be enabled for this project even if
    the Windows App SDK Nuget package has not yet been restored.
  -->
  <PropertyGroup Condition="'$(DisableHasPackageAndPublishMenuAddedByProject)'!='true' and '$(EnableMsixTooling)'=='true'">
    <HasPackageAndPublishMenu>true</HasPackageAndPublishMenu>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <!-- Publish Properties -->
  <PropertyGroup>
    <PublishReadyToRun Condition="'$(Configuration)' == 'Debug'">False</PublishReadyToRun>

    <PublishTrimmed Condition="'$(Configuration)' == 'Debug'">False</PublishTrimmed>
    <PublishTrimmed Condition="'$(Configuration)' != 'Debug'">True</PublishTrimmed>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>

toolResult.textResultForLlm: ## Diagnosing Startup CrashesA packaged WinUI 3 app can build cleanly and still crash the instant it launches — `winapp run` returns no usable window and the process is gone. The build log and the analyzer cannot see this; only a real launch does. The **wrong** way to chase it is to sprinkle `File.WriteAllText` traces through `Program.cs` / `App.xaml.cs` and re-run repeatedly — that burns time and usually misses the real frame (the crash often happens in native activation, before your managed `Main` even runs).**Capture the real exception first.** Either run the launch-and-diagnose helper:```powershell & "/scripts/Test-AppLaunch.ps1" -Target "" ```…or read the Windows **Application** event log directly for the two events the crash writes:```powershell Get-WinEvent -LogName Application -MaxEvents 40 | Where-Object { $_.Id -in 1000,1026 -and $_.TimeCreated -gt (Get-Date).AddMinutes(-3) } | ForEach-Object { "`n=== Event $($_.Id) @ $($_.TimeCreated) ==="; $_.Message } ```- **Event 1000** — faulting module + native **Exception code** (e.g. `0x8001010E`). - **Event 1026** — *.NET Runtime*: the managed **exception type, message, and stack**. This is the one that names the actual throwing frame. Read it before changing any code.**Known native codes and what they usually mean** (the code names the error *class*; the real fix is whatever the captured stack points at):| Exception code | Meaning | Usual migration cause → where to look | |---|---|---| | `0x80004003` | `E_POINTER` | Static-window **init-order race** — a `Page` read `App.MainWindow` (or another static window reference) before `OnLaunched` assigned it. Keep `MainWindow`'s constructor inert and navigate after `Activate`. See [Initialization order](#windowing). | | `0x8001010E` | `RPC_E_WRONG_THREAD` | A **thread/apartment-affined object** was accessed during startup — commonly a view- or `CoreWindow`-affined UWP API touched from a `static` initializer, a type constructor, or off the UI thread. Construct/access it on the UI thread *after* `Activate`. If the API has no WinUI 3 desktop equivalent, defer it. | | `0xE0434352` | Managed CLR exception | Read the **.NET exception type** in event 1026. `TypeLoadException` / `FileNotFoundException` almost always means a missing or version-incompatible package reference, not your code. | | `0xC000027B` | Native stowed exception | Often a legacy projection/activation incompatibility for an API used at startup. If the API/contract is unsupported on the current OS, defer it. |> Do **not** assume the entry point is the problem. A custom `Program.Main` for WinUI 3 **correctly** carries `[STAThread]` + `ComWrappersSupport.InitializeComWrappers()` + the `DispatcherQueueSynchronizationContext` setup — this matches the SDK's auto-generated `Main`. `[STAThread]` is **required**, not a bug. If you have a hand-written entry point and don't need single-instancing/redirection, the simplest path is to delete it and let the SDK generate `Main`.The Step 4 validator runs this same check (`Validate-UwpMigration.ps1` Section 7) and **fails** when the app registers but dies at startup, surfacing the captured signature in `.validator-diagnostics.txt`.

The crash is in `Microsoft.UI.Xaml.dll` with exception code `0xc000027b`. This is the faulting module during XAML parsing/initialization. There's no .NET event 1026 - this is a native crash.

I need to find what XAML issue is causing the crash. The crash happens in the XAML subsystem during initialization.

Common causes:
1. A XAML element referencing a resource that doesn't exist
2. A style key that's not defined
3. A namespace or type that can't be resolved
4. An unsupported XAML feature

Since the crash is in Microsoft.UI.Xaml.dll at startup, it's likely a XAML parse error. 

I'm checking the MainPage.xaml and scenario files - the migration likely left references to UWP styles like `SampleHeaderTextStyle`, `ScenarioDescriptionTextStyle`, `TagLineTextStyle`, `CopyrightTextStyle`, `HyperlinkStyle`, `SeparatorStyle`, and `SymbolButton` that don't exist in WinUI 3, which would cause the parser to fail.

data.reasoningText:
No event 1026 (no managed exception). The crash is purely native in `Microsoft.UI.Xaml.dll`. The same fault offset `0x00000000003ad79d` in `Microsoft.UI.Xaml.dll`. 

This is interesting - the same exact crash offset. This suggests the crash happens at the same code path in the XAML engine regardless of the resource fix.

Let me look at the App.xaml again. The BasedOn style might be causing the issue - `BasedOn="{StaticResource SubtitleTextBlockStyle}"` inside an App.xaml that also merges `XamlControlsResources`. The `SubtitleTextBlockStyle` is defined in the WinUI 3 control resources.


The resource merge order could be the culprit here - even though `XamlControlsResources` is merged before the style definition, the `BasedOn` reference might fail during initialization if the theme resources haven't loaded yet. In WinUI 3, styles that reference other styles through `BasedOn` can be problematic during app startup when the theme system is still initializing.

I think the more reliable approach is to bypass `BasedOn` entirely and directly replace those style references in the scenario XAML files with the built-in WinUI 3 styles instead. It's more tedious across the seven scenario files, but it avoids the initialization timing issue altogether.

Before I go down that path though, I should verify whether the App.xaml styles are actually what's causing the crash at that specific offset, or if something else is triggering it. Let me strip out the custom styles from App.xaml temporarily and see if the app even launches without them.

The UIA dump for Scenario 2 shows only 66 elements and the tree is quite shallow. Looking at the tree, after the Window element there are children:
- Non Client Input Sink Window
- AppWindow Custom Title Bar
- DesktopChildSiteBridge ← this should contain all the actual content

This means the UIA dump has the content, but it's not being properly traversed to find the `mediaPlayerElement`.

The issue is that the `MediaPlayerElement` control itself doesn't expose an `automationId="mediaPlayerElement"` through the UIA tree - instead, only its transport controls (like `MediaControlsCommandBar`) are visible in UIA.

But Scenario 1 PASSES (2/2 including `mediaPlayerElement`). 

Looking at the control definition, it's just a basic MediaPlayerElement with no special properties. S1 passes while S2 fails even though both have the same control, so the difference must be in what else is present on the page - S1 has a "Load" button alongside the mediaPlayerElement, and for it to pass 2/2, both controls must be getting found somehow. I need to figure out how "mediaPlayerElement" is actually being matched in the UIA tree.

toolResult.textResultForLlm:
1. <#
2. .SYNOPSIS
3. Grade a migrated WinUI 3 app's functional parity against the UWP feature
4. checklist. Deterministic structural gate (exit 0 = PASS, 1 = FAIL) plus a
5. human/LLM-readable PARITY-REPORT.md that drives the agent's fix loop.
6. 
7. .DESCRIPTION
8. Layered comparison (cheap + robust first, no pixel diff — none of the toolchain
9. ships ImageMagick, and a screenshot-byte diff is fragile across theme/DPI):
10. 
11.   L1  Reachability — did the WinUI 3 capture produce a non-blank screenshot for
12.       each baseline scenario? (blank window == failed migration; mirrors the
13.       benchmark's own blank-screenshot penalty.)
14.   L2  Control coverage — for each baseline scenario, what fraction of its named
15.       / labelled controls appear (by AutomationId, name, or label text) in the
16.       WinUI 3 scenario's captured UIA dump? This is the primary structural signal.
17. 
18. Per-scenario verdict:
19.   - pass    : reachable AND coverage >= -PassThreshold (default 0.8)
20.   - partial : reachable AND coverage >= -PartialThreshold (default 0.4)
21.   - fail    : not reachable, blank screenshot, or coverage below partial
22. 
23. The script exits non-zero if ANY scenario is `fail` (or, with -StrictPartial,
24. if any is below `pass`). Visual fidelity + behavioural nuance are intentionally
25. left to the agent (it has the screenshots) / the benchmark judge — this gate
26. catches the dominant failure mode: silently dropped scenarios and controls.
27. 
28. .PARAMETER Checklist
29. Baseline checklist.json (from Extract-UwpFeatureChecklist.ps1).
30. 
31. .PARAMETER Candidate
32. Folder produced by Capture-AppScenarios.ps1 against the WinUI 3 app (contains
33. ui/ + screenshots/ + capture-manifest.json).
34. 
35. .PARAMETER OutDir
36. Where to write PARITY-REPORT.md + parity-result.json. Defaults to -Candidate.
37. 
38. .PARAMETER PassThreshold
39. Coverage fraction for a `pass`. Default 0.8.
40. 
41. .PARAMETER PartialThreshold
42. Coverage fraction for a `partial`. Default 0.4.
43. 
44. .PARAMETER BlankBytes
45. Screenshots at/under this size are treated as blank/unrendered. Default 15360.
46. 
47. .PARAMETER StrictPartial
48. Treat `partial` scenarios as failures for the exit code.
49. 
50. .EXAMPLE
51. .\Compare-Parity.ps1 -Checklist .\parity-baseline\checklist.json -Candidate .\parity-winui3
52. #>
53. [CmdletBinding()]
54. param(
55.     [Parameter(Mandatory)][string]$Checklist,
56.     [Parameter(Mandatory)][string]$Candidate,
57.     [string]$OutDir,
58.     [double]$PassThreshold = 0.8,
59.     [double]$PartialThreshold = 0.4,
60.     [int]$BlankBytes = 15360,
61.     [switch]$StrictPartial
62. )
63. 
64. $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
65. if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $Checklist)) { throw "Checklist not found: $Checklist" }
66. if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $Candidate)) { throw "Candidate capture folder not found: $Candidate" }
67. $Candidate = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath $Candidate).ProviderPath
68. if (-not $OutDir) { $OutDir = $Candidate }
69. if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $OutDir)) { New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $OutDir -Force | Out-Null }
70. 
71. $cl = Get-Content -LiteralPath $Checklist -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json
72. $uiDir   = Join-Path $Candidate 'ui'
73. $shotDir = Join-Path $Candidate 'screenshots'
74. 
75. function Test-Token([string]$haystack, [string]$token) {
76.     if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($token)) { return $false }
77.     # Normalize whitespace and case for substring match.
78.     $t = ($token -replace '\s+', ' ').Trim()
79.     if ($t.Length -lt 2) { return $false }
80.     return $haystack.ToLowerInvariant().Contains($t.ToLowerInvariant())
81. }
82. 
83. $scenarioResults = @()
84. foreach ($s in $cl.scenarios) {
85.     $num = [int]$s.number
86.     $uiFile = Join-Path $uiDir ('{0:00}.json' -f $num)
87.     $shotFile = Join-Path $shotDir ('{0:00}_{1}.png' -f $num, $s.slug)
88. 
89.     $uiText = ''
90.     if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $uiFile) { $uiText = Get-Content -LiteralPath $uiFile -Raw }
91. 
92.     $shotBytes = if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $shotFile) { (Get-Item -LiteralPath $shotFile).Length } else { 0 }
93.     $reachable = ($shotBytes -gt $BlankBytes) -or ($uiText.Length -gt 200)
94.     $blank = ($shotBytes -gt 0 -and $shotBytes -le $BlankBytes)
95. 
96.     # Control coverage: a control counts as "present" if its AutomationId, name,
97.     # or label text appears in the captured UIA dump.
98.     $controls = @($s.controls)
99.     $total = $controls.Count
100.     $hits = 0
101.     $missing = @()
102.     foreach ($c in $controls) {
103.         $found = $false
104.         foreach ($tok in @($c.name, $c.label)) {
105.             if (Test-Token $uiText $tok) { $found = $true; break }
106.         }
107.         if ($found) { $hits++ }
108.         else {
109.             $desc = $c.type
110.             if ($c.label) { $desc += " `"$($c.label)`"" } elseif ($c.name) { $desc += " ($($c.name))" }
111.             $missing += $desc
112.         }
113.     }
114.     $coverage = if ($total -eq 0) { 1.0 } else { [math]::Round($hits / $total, 3) }
115. 
116.     $verdict =
117.         if (-not $reachable) { 'fail' }
118.         elseif ($coverage -ge $PassThreshold) { 'pass' }
119.         elseif ($coverage -ge $PartialThreshold) { 'partial' }
120.         else { 'fail' }
121. 
122.     $reason = ''
123.     if (-not $reachable) {
124.         $reason = if ($blank) { "Scenario screenshot is blank ($shotBytes bytes) — page did not render." } else { "Scenario not reachable — no screenshot/UIA captured." }
125.     } elseif ($missing.Count -gt 0) {
126.         $reason = "Missing $($missing.Count)/$total control(s): " + (($missing | Select-Object -First 8) -join '; ')
127.     }
128. 
129.     $scenarioResults += [PSCustomObject]@{
130.         number = $num; title = $s.title; verdict = $verdict
131.         coverage = $coverage; controlsTotal = $total; controlsFound = $hits
132.         reachable = $reachable; screenshotBytes = $shotBytes
133.         missing = $missing; reason = $reason
134.         screenshot = ('{0:00}_{1}.png' -f $num, $s.slug)
135.     }
136. }
137. 
138. $counts = @{ pass = 0; partial = 0; fail = 0 }
139. foreach ($r in $scenarioResults) { $counts[$r.verdict]++ }
140. $totalScenarios = $scenarioResults.Count
141. # Parity score: pass=1, partial=0.5, fail=0.
142. $parityScore = if ($totalScenarios -eq 0) { 0 } else {
143.     [math]::Round((($counts.pass * 1.0) + ($counts.partial * 0.5)) / $totalScenarios * 100, 1)
144. }
145. 
146. $failGate = ($counts.fail -gt 0) -or ($StrictPartial -and $counts.partial -gt 0)
147. 
148. # ─── PARITY-REPORT.md ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
149. $md = New-Object System.Collections.Generic.List[string]
150. [void]$md.Add("# Parity Report — $($cl.featureName)")
151. [void]$md.Add('')

1. <#
2. .SYNOPSIS
3. Grade a migrated WinUI 3 app's functional parity against the UWP feature
4. checklist. Deterministic structural gate (exit 0 = PASS, 1 = FAIL) plus a
5. human/LLM-readable PARITY-REPORT.md that drives the agent's fix loop.
6. 
7. .DESCRIPTION
8. Layered comparison (cheap + robust first, no pixel diff — none of the toolchain
9. ships ImageMagick, and a screenshot-byte diff is fragile across theme/DPI):
10. 
11.   L1  Reachability — did the WinUI 3 capture produce a non-blank screenshot for
12.       each baseline scenario? (blank window == failed migration; mirrors the
13.       benchmark's own blank-screenshot penalty.)
14.   L2  Control coverage — for each baseline scenario, what fraction of its named
15.       / labelled controls appear (by AutomationId, name, or label text) in the
16.       WinUI 3 scenario's captured UIA dump? This is the primary structural signal.
17. 
18. Per-scenario verdict:
19.   - pass    : reachable AND coverage >= -PassThreshold (default 0.8)
20.   - partial : reachable AND coverage >= -PartialThreshold (default 0.4)
21.   - fail    : not reachable, blank screenshot, or coverage below partial
22. 
23. The script exits non-zero if ANY scenario is `fail` (or, with -StrictPartial,
24. if any is below `pass`). Visual fidelity + behavioural nuance are intentionally
25. left to the agent (it has the screenshots) / the benchmark judge — this gate
26. catches the dominant failure mode: silently dropped scenarios and controls.
27. 
28. .PARAMETER Checklist
29. Baseline checklist.json (from Extract-UwpFeatureChecklist.ps1).
30. 
31. .PARAMETER Candidate
32. Folder produced by Capture-AppScenarios.ps1 against the WinUI 3 app (contains
33. ui/ + screenshots/ + capture-manifest.json).
34. 
35. .PARAMETER OutDir
36. Where to write PARITY-REPORT.md + parity-result.json. Defaults to -Candidate.
37. 
38. .PARAMETER PassThreshold
39. Coverage fraction for a `pass`. Default 0.8.
40. 
41. .PARAMETER PartialThreshold
42. Coverage fraction for a `partial`. Default 0.4.
43. 
44. .PARAMETER BlankBytes
45. Screenshots at/under this size are treated as blank/unrendered. Default 15360.
46. 
47. .PARAMETER StrictPartial
48. Treat `partial` scenarios as failures for the exit code.
49. 
50. .EXAMPLE
51. .\Compare-Parity.ps1 -Checklist .\parity-baseline\checklist.json -Candidate .\parity-winui3
52. #>
53. [CmdletBinding()]
54. param(
55.     [Parameter(Mandatory)][string]$Checklist,
56.     [Parameter(Mandatory)][string]$Candidate,
57.     [string]$OutDir,
58.     [double]$PassThreshold = 0.8,
59.     [double]$PartialThreshold = 0.4,
60.     [int]$BlankBytes = 15360,
61.     [switch]$StrictPartial
62. )
63. 
64. $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
65. if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $Checklist)) { throw "Checklist not found: $Checklist" }
66. if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $Candidate)) { throw "Candidate capture folder not found: $Candidate" }
67. $Candidate = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath $Candidate).ProviderPath
68. if (-not $OutDir) { $OutDir = $Candidate }
69. if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $OutDir)) { New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $OutDir -Force | Out-Null }
70. 
71. $cl = Get-Content -LiteralPath $Checklist -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json
72. $uiDir   = Join-Path $Candidate 'ui'
73. $shotDir = Join-Path $Candidate 'screenshots'
74. 
75. function Test-Token([string]$haystack, [string]$token) {
76.     if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($token)) { return $false }
77.     # Normalize whitespace and case for substring match.
78.     $t = ($token -replace '\s+', ' ').Trim()
79.     if ($t.Length -lt 2) { return $false }
80.     return $haystack.ToLowerInvariant().Contains($t.ToLowerInvariant())
81. }
82. 
83. $scenarioResults = @()
84. foreach ($s in $cl.scenarios) {
85.     $num = [int]$s.number
86.     $uiFile = Join-Path $uiDir ('{0:00}.json' -f $num)
87.     $shotFile = Join-Path $shotDir ('{0:00}_{1}.png' -f $num, $s.slug)
88. 
89.     $uiText = ''
90.     if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $uiFile) { $uiText = Get-Content -LiteralPath $uiFile -Raw }
91. 
92.     $shotBytes = if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $shotFile) { (Get-Item -LiteralPath $shotFile).Length } else { 0 }
93.     $reachable = ($shotBytes -gt $BlankBytes) -or ($uiText.Length -gt 200)
94.     $blank = ($shotBytes -gt 0 -and $shotBytes -le $BlankBytes)
95. 
96.     # Control coverage: a control counts as "present" if its AutomationId, name,
97.     # or label text appears in the captured UIA dump.
98.     $controls = @($s.controls)
99.     $total = $controls.Count
100.     $hits = 0
101.     $missing = @()
102.     foreach ($c in $controls) {
103.         $found = $false
104.         foreach ($tok in @($c.name, $c.label)) {
105.             if (Test-Token $uiText $tok) { $found = $true; break }
106.         }
107.         if ($found) { $hits++ }
108.         else {
109.             $desc = $c.type
110.             if ($c.label) { $desc += " `"$($c.label)`"" } elseif ($c.name) { $desc += " ($($c.name))" }
111.             $missing += $desc
112.         }
113.     }
114.     $coverage = if ($total -eq 0) { 1.0 } else { [math]::Round($hits / $total, 3) }
115. 
116.     $verdict =
117.         if (-not $reachable) { 'fail' }
118.         elseif ($coverage -ge $PassThreshold) { 'pass' }
119.         elseif ($coverage -ge $PartialThreshold) { 'partial' }
120.         else { 'fail' }
121. 
122.     $reason = ''
123.     if (-not $reachable) {
124.         $reason = if ($blank) { "Scenario screenshot is blank ($shotBytes bytes) — page did not render." } else { "Scenario not reachable — no screenshot/UIA captured." }
125.     } elseif ($missing.Count -gt 0) {
126.         $reason = "Missing $($missing.Count)/$total control(s): " + (($missing | Select-Object -First 8) -join '; ')
127.     }
128. 
129.     $scenarioResults += [PSCustomObject]@{
130.         number = $num; title = $s.title; verdict = $verdict
131.         coverage = $coverage; controlsTotal = $total; controlsFound = $hits
132.         reachable = $reachable; screenshotBytes = $shotBytes
133.         missing = $missing; reason = $reason
134.         screenshot = ('{0:00}_{1}.png' -f $num, $s.slug)
135.     }
136. }
137. 
138. $counts = @{ pass = 0; partial = 0; fail = 0 }
139. foreach ($r in $scenarioResults) { $counts[$r.verdict]++ }
140. $totalScenarios = $scenarioResults.Count
141. # Parity score: pass=1, partial=0.5, fail=0.
142. $parityScore = if ($totalScenarios -eq 0) { 0 } else {
143.     [math]::Round((($counts.pass * 1.0) + ($counts.partial * 0.5)) / $totalScenarios * 100, 1)
144. }
145. 
146. $failGate = ($counts.fail -gt 0) -or ($StrictPartial -and $counts.partial -gt 0)
147. 
148. # ─── PARITY-REPORT.md ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
149. $md = New-Object System.Collections.Generic.List[string]
150. [void]$md.Add("# Parity Report — $($cl.featureName)")
151. [void]$md.Add('')
152. [void]$md.Add("Generated $((Get-Date).ToString('o')) by Compare-Parity.ps1.")
153. [void]$md.Add('')
154. [void]$md.Add("**Parity score: $parityScore / 100**  ·  pass=$($counts.pass) partial=$($counts.partial) fail=$($counts.fail)  ·  $totalScenarios scenario(s)")
155. [void]$md.Add('')
156. [void]$md.Add('| # | Scenario | Verdict | Coverage | Screenshot | Notes |')
157. [void]$md.Add('|---|----------|---------|----------|------------|-------|')
158. foreach ($r in $scenarioResults) {
159.     $cov = if ($r.controlsTotal -eq 0) { 'n/a' } else { "$($r.controlsFound)/$($r.controlsTotal)" }
160.     $note = ($r.reason -replace '\|', '\\|')
161.     [void]$md.Add("| $($r.number) | $($r.title) | $($r.verdict.ToUpper()) | $cov | $($r.screenshot) | $note |")
162. }
163. [void]$md.Add('')
164. $failing = @($scenarioResults | Where-Object { $_.verdict -ne 'pass' })
165. if ($failing.Count -gt 0) {
166.     [void]$md.Add('## Scenarios needing work')
167.     [void]$md.Add('')
168.     foreach ($r in $failing) {
169.         [void]$md.Add("### Scenario $($r.number) — $($r.title)  [$($r.verdict.ToUpper())]")
170.         [void]$md.Add('')
171.         if ($r.reason) { [void]$md.Add("- $($r.reason)") }
172.         if ($r.missing.Count -gt 0) {
173.             [void]$md.Add('- Controls not found in the WinUI 3 UIA tree:')
174.             foreach ($m in $r.missing) { [void]$md.Add("  - $m") }
175.         }
176.         [void]$md.Add("- Inspect: ``winapp ui inspect -a <PID> --interactive`` after navigating to this scenario, and compare ``screenshots/$($r.screenshot)`` against the baseline.")
177.         [void]$md.Add('')
178.     }
179. } else {
180.     [void]$md.Add('All scenarios reached `pass`. ✔')
181.     [void]$md.Add('')
182. }
183. [void]$md.Add('> Coverage is a structural proxy (AutomationId / name / label text found in the')
184. [void]$md.Add('> captured UIA tree). A `pass` here is necessary but not sufficient: also confirm')
185. [void]$md.Add('> visually (screenshots) and behaviourally that each control does what the UWP')
186. [void]$md.Add('> source does. Set `AutomationProperties.AutomationId` on controls to make this')
187. [void]$md.Add('> check reliable.')
188. 
189. $reportPath = Join-Path $OutDir 'PARITY-REPORT.md'
190. Set-Content -LiteralPath $reportPath -Value $md -Encoding UTF8
191. 
192. $resultJson = [ordered]@{
193.     featureName  = $cl.featureName
194.     parityScore  = $parityScore
195.     counts       = $counts
196.     totalScenarios = $totalScenarios
197.     pass         = (-not $failGate)
198.     thresholds   = @{ pass = $PassThreshold; partial = $PartialThreshold; strictPartial = [bool]$StrictPartial }
199.     scenarios    = @($scenarioResults)
200. }
201. $resultPath = Join-Path $OutDir 'parity-result.json'
202. $resultJson | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 8 | Set-Content -LiteralPath $resultPath -Encoding UTF8
203. 
204. # ─── stdout summary ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
205. Write-Host ""
206. Write-Host "==> Compare-Parity"
207. Write-Host "    Feature : $($cl.featureName)"
208. Write-Host "    Score   : $parityScore / 100  (pass=$($counts.pass) partial=$($counts.partial) fail=$($counts.fail))"
209. foreach ($r in $scenarioResults) {
210.     $cov = if ($r.controlsTotal -eq 0) { 'n/a  ' } else { ('{0}/{1}' -f $r.controlsFound, $r.controlsTotal) }
211.     Write-Host ("    [{0,-7}] {1,2}. {2}  ({3})" -f $r.verdict, $r.number, $r.title, $cov)
212. }
213. Write-Host "    Report  : $reportPath"
214. Write-Host ""
215. if ($failGate) {
216.     Write-Host "==> Compare-Parity: FAIL — $($counts.fail) scenario(s) failed$(if($StrictPartial){" / $($counts.partial) partial"}). Fix and re-capture."
217.     exit 1
218. } else {

                <Grid.ColumnDefinitions>

                    <ColumnDefinition/>
                    <ColumnDefinition/>

            </Grid>


            <StackPanel x:Name="DiscreteControls" Orientation="Horizontal" HorizontalAlignment="Center" VerticalAlignment="Top">
                <Button x:Name="LogCurrentTimeCorrelation" Content="Log Times" Click="LogCurrentTimeCorrelation_Click" />
                <Button x:Name ="GoToStart" Content="GoToStart" Click="GoToStart_Click" />
                <Button Tag="-00:15:00" Content="<<15m" Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>
                <Button Tag="-00:05:00" Content="<<5m" Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>
                <Button Tag="-00:00:30" Content="<<30s" Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>
                <Button Tag="-00:00:02" Content="<<2s" Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>
                <Button x:Name="PlayButton" IsEnabled="False" Click="Play_Click">
                    <SymbolIcon x:Name="PlayIcon" Symbol="Play"/>
                </Button>
                <Button x:Name="PauseButton" IsEnabled="False" Click="Pause_Click">
                    <SymbolIcon x:Name="PauseIcon" Symbol="Pause"/>
                </Button>
                <Button Tag="00:00:02" Content="2s>>"  Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>
                <Button Tag="00:00:30" Content="30s>>" Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>
                <Button Tag="00:05:00" Content="5m>>" Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>
                <Button Tag="00:15:00" Content="15m>>" Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>
                <Button x:Name ="GoToLive" Content="GoToLive" Click="GoToLive_Click" />
            </StackPanel>
        </StackPanel>

        <logging:LogView x:Name="LoggerControl" Grid.Row="3" Margin="0,10,0,0"/>
    </Grid>
</Page>

                    <ColumnDefinition/>
                    <ColumnDefinition/>
                    <ColumnDefinition/>

            </Grid>

            <Grid x:Name="PositionUpdateControls" Margin="0,10,0,0" HorizontalAlignment="Center" >
                <Grid.RowDefinitions>
                    <RowDefinition/>
                    <RowDefinition/>
                    <RowDefinition/>

                <Grid.ColumnDefinitions>
                    <ColumnDefinition/>
                    <ColumnDefinition/>
                    <ColumnDefinition/>
                </Grid.ColumnDefinitions>

                <TextBlock Text="StartPosition" Margin="10,0" Grid.Row="0" Grid.Column="0" HorizontalAlignment="Center" />
                <TextBlock x:Name="StartPosition" Text="Start" Margin="10,0" Grid.Row="1" Grid.Column="0" HorizontalAlignment="Center" />

            </Grid>


            <StackPanel x:Name="DiscreteControls" Orientation="Horizontal" HorizontalAlignment="Center" VerticalAlignment="Top">
                <Button x:Name="LogCurrentTimeCorrelation" Content="Log Times" Click="LogCurrentTimeCorrelation_Click" />
                <Button x:Name ="GoToStart" Content="GoToStart" Click="GoToStart_Click" />
                <Button AutomationProperties.AutomationId="seek-back-15m" Tag="-00:15:00" Content="<<15m" Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>

                <Button AutomationProperties.AutomationId="seek-back-2s" Tag="-00:00:02" Content="<<2s" Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>
                <Button x:Name="PlayButton" IsEnabled="False" Click="Play_Click">
                    <SymbolIcon x:Name="PlayIcon" Symbol="Play"/>
                </Button>
                <Button x:Name="PauseButton" IsEnabled="False" Click="Pause_Click">
                    <SymbolIcon x:Name="PauseIcon" Symbol="Pause"/>
                </Button>
                <Button Tag="00:00:02" Content="2s>>"  Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>
                <Button Tag="00:00:30" Content="30s>>" Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>
                <Button Tag="00:05:00" Content="5m>>" Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>
                <Button Tag="00:15:00" Content="15m>>" Click="SeekFixedAmount_Click"/>

            </StackPanel>
        </StackPanel>

    </Grid>
</Page>
